intro: The third movement of the Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90, is in C minor and opens with a melody in the cellos. When the melody returns, a solo horn plays it and the cellos play a new line beneath it.

sections.label: A · C-minor melody in the cellos
sections.mNote: C-minor melody over plucked basses and violin figuration

sections.label: B · Wind chords across the beat
sections.mNote: A♭ minor and major alternate over syncopated cellos.

relations.label: The C minor song returns
relations.basis: The ternary movement restores its opening song after the middle section, with changed scoring; the matched phrases lie inside the opening A and the A′ section marked near 214 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.937, sustained 30 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 218.5 s (cache/form/brahms-3-poco-allegretto.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening theme, cellos
cues.text: The cellos play the melody high in their range, softly, in C minor. Above them the two violin sections alternate in triplet figures, and the double basses play pizzicato. The phrasing of the melody crosses the bar lines of the three-beat metre.
cues.evidence: Brahms, Symphony No. 3, III, bars 1–12; Breitkopf & Härtel collected edition, IMSLP 317593. Scoring and phrasing: Kelly Dean Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Cello entry in major
cues.text: Before the cadence in C minor has finished, the cellos begin a phrase in major, marked dolce. The first violins join them a sixth above. The bass holds C while the melody runs across the bar lines.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 24–31; Hansen’s score guide describes the overlapping cello entry, violin harmony and C pedal. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Wiesbaden, summer 1883
cues.text: In the summer of 1883 Brahms interrupted a trip along the Rhine and rented rooms in Wiesbaden to finish the Third Symphony. He was fifty. Six years had passed since the Second.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note: composition in Wiesbaden in summer 1883, following the Second Symphony of 1877. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3

cues.title: Tied wind chords, bars 54–61
cues.text: In bars 54–61 the winds hold their chords across the bar lines, so the upbeat is heard as the downbeat. A♭ minor alternates with A♭ major. Between the chords the cellos play a syncopated descent from A♭ to E♭.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 54–61; Hansen’s score guide identifies the displaced wind chords and cello descent. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: String passage in B major
cues.text: The winds stop. The strings play a swaying melody in B major, and the downbeat is clear again. As the phrase rises, the double basses play with the bow for the first time in the movement, after playing only pizzicato until now.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 70–78; first bowed double-bass entry and B-major string passage described in Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First performance, Vienna, 1883
cues.text: Hans Richter conducted the Vienna Philharmonic in the première on 2 December 1883. According to the critic Eduard Hanslick, Richter had called the new symphony “Brahms’s Eroica” shortly before. All four movements end quietly, this one included.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note: première by the Vienna Philharmonic under Hans Richter on 2 December 1883, Hanslick on Richter’s “Brahms’s Eroica”, and the quiet endings of all four movements. https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3

cues.title: Reprise, solo horn
cues.text: A solo horn plays the opening theme again in C minor. Beneath it the cellos, no longer carrying the melody, play wide rising arpeggios.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 98–110: horn reprise with cello arpeggios. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Melody in the solo oboe
cues.text: After the horn, a solo oboe takes the melody that the first violins played the first time. Below it the cellos continue their wide upward arpeggios. The violins now divide the rippling triplets between them.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 111–122: the oboe takes the melody that the first violins had in bars 13–23, over cello arpeggios. Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html . Mandel lists the successive solo instruments: https://www.bso.org/works/brahms-symphony-no-3
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Melody in violins and cellos
cues.text: At bars 139–149 the first violins and cellos play the melody across three octaves. The clarinets join the accompaniment, and flute, oboe and horns take the shorter subsidiary phrases.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 139–149; Hansen details the redistribution of melody and accompaniment. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Coda, bars 150–163
cues.text: The wind chords from the middle section return, still crossing the bar lines. This time they lead back to C minor. After a final swell, the strings play pizzicato beneath the held last chord.
cues.evidence: Third Symphony, III, coda, bars 150–163; Hansen describes the recalled wind chords, final swell and pizzicato close. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: A♭ minor interrupts the C-minor cadence
transitions.from: A · C-minor melody in the cellos
transitions.to: B · Wind chords across the beat
transitions.how: An A♭-minor chord follows the C-minor cadence within the same bar. The winds hold across the bar line, and the cellos play a syncopated descent towards E♭. The written metre remains 3/8, but the chord changes put the stress on the upbeats so that they sound like downbeats.
transitions.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 49–61; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html.

transitions.title: Opening motif rises in sequence to C
transitions.from: B · Wind chords across the beat
transitions.to: A′ · The horn sings the song
transitions.how: Clarinet and bassoon play the song’s first three notes in A♭ minor, then in B♭ minor, over chromatic string chords. The sequence reaches C minor. Flute and oboe lengthen the notes and the horns hold C. The solo horn then plays the complete melody above new cello arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 93–110; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html.

transitions.title: The wind chords return
transitions.from: A′ · The horn sings the song
transitions.to: Coda · Wind chords, then C minor
transitions.how: In bars 150–163, after the song’s C-minor cadence, the winds play again the chords that led into the middle section. Their harmony takes an A♭-minor colouring, then moves back towards C. The strings join them on a diminished seventh. A rising phrase extends across the 3/8 bars, and three descending chords close the passage.
transitions.evidence: Third Symphony, III, bars 150–163; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus90.html.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
